memory: I've learned to be more intentional about my health as I've gotten older. It's the little things that add up - like taking care of my joints, getting enough rest, and managing my energy levels. Adjusting my routine to the changing seasons in Kansas helps me feel my best. I used to take my health for granted, but now I make sure to prioritize self-care and make choices that support my overall well-being.I've learned to be more mindful of my diet as I've gotten older. My metabolism has slowed down, and I need to be more careful about what I eat to maintain my weight. I focus on consuming more protein, healthy fats, and fiber to keep my digestion in check. Processed foods can make me feel sluggish, so I try to cook most of my meals at home. One of my favorite go-to meals is grilled salmon with roasted vegetables - it's simple, delicious, and packed with nutrients that help with inflammation.I've learned that consistency is key when it comes to exercise. I used to think that intense workouts were the only way to get results, but now I understand that regular, gentle exercise is more important. I make sure to walk every day, no matter the weather, and I've also started incorporating strength training into my routine. My doctor told me that muscle loss accelerates with age, so maintaining strength is crucial for preventing injuries. I do light weightlifting and resistance band exercises a few times a week, which has greatly improved my balance and joint health.I've learned the importance of prioritizing sleep as I've gotten older. I used to be able to get by on less sleep, but now I need a solid seven or eight hours to feel my best. To improve my sleep hygiene, I've made sure to avoid screens an hour before bed, keep my bedroom cool and dark, and establish a consistent sleep schedule. Additionally, I've started taking magnesium supplements, which have been a game-changer for relaxation. It's amazing how something as simple as getting enough sleep can make such a significant difference in how I feel.I've learned to prioritize skin care as I've gotten older. I used to not worry about it as much, but now I understand the importance of hydration and sun protection. I wear SPF every day, even in the winter, because sun damage can add up over the years. I also drink a lot of water, which helps keep my skin from feeling dry, especially during Kansas winters. Additionally, I've started using a retinol cream at night, which is said to be great for keeping skin healthy as you age. It's not about looking 30 again, but about maintaining healthy and radiant skin.I've learned the importance of nurturing social connections as I've gotten older. It's easy to get caught up in work, family, and responsibilities, but having a strong support system is crucial for mental well-being. I make it a point to have coffee with friends at least once a week and joined a book club last year. It's been a great way to stay engaged and meet new people. I truly believe that staying socially active helps keep me young and vibrant.I've learned the importance of keeping my mind active as I've gotten older. I used to think that memory loss was inevitable, but now I understand that it's possible to slow down cognitive decline with mental stimulation. I make sure to do puzzles, read books, and even learn new skills to keep my brain sharp. I recently started taking an online class on art history just for fun, and it's been a great mental exercise. I believe that lifelong learning is key to maintaining cognitive function, so I'm committed to continuing my education and staying engaged.I've learned to be more proactive about managing chronic pain as I've gotten older. My osteoarthritis tends to act up more in the colder months, and some days, my joints feel stiff no matter what I do. I've found that warm baths with Epsom salts help to alleviate the discomfort, and I also swear by using a heating pad in the mornings. My doctor recommended that I try tai chi or gentle stretching, so I've been looking into that as well. It's a process of finding ways to manage the pain so that I can continue doing the things I love. Aging isn't about avoiding discomfort altogether; it's about learning to navigate it and find ways to stay active and engaged.I've learned to embrace aging as a natural part of life. While there are certainly challenges that come with it, I've also gained so much wisdom and insight from my experiences. I've learned to listen to my body, prioritize self-care, and appreciate the small joys in life. If I could offer advice to my younger self, I would say: don't stress about the little things, take care of your health early on, and enjoy every stage of life. Aging is not something to fear; it's just another chapter in the story of life. I'm excited to see what the future holds!I've been keeping track of my medical test reports over the years, and it's interesting to see how things have changed. I always try to stay on top of my health by getting regular check-ups, especially with my history of diabetes and hypertension. My latest bloodwork had some ups and downs, but nothing too alarming. Living in Kansas, where the seasons affect everything from my energy levels to my joint pain, I've learned to keep a close eye on my numbers so I can adjust my lifestyle as needed.Let me break it down for you. My most recent fasting blood glucose test came back at 135 mg/dL, which is a bit higher than I'd like—it should ideally be under 100 mg/dL. My A1C was 6.9%, which is just above the target range of 6.5%, meaning I need to be more careful with my carb intake. My doctor suggested adding more fiber to my diet and making sure I get some light exercise after meals. I've also been checking my blood sugar at home, and my morning readings tend to hover around 125-130 mg/dL.My cholesterol numbers were a mixed bag. My total cholesterol was 195 mg/dL, which is okay, but my LDL(bad cholesterol) was 130 mg/dL—higher than the recommended under 100 mg/dL. On the bright side, my HDL(good cholesterol) was 58 mg/dL, which is in a good range. My triglycerides were 140 mg/dL, which is slightly elevated but not too concerning. My doctor advised me to increase my intake of healthy fats like avocados and nuts and to cut back on saturated fats.Blood pressure has always been something I need to monitor. At my last check-up, my reading was 138/85 mmHg, which is on the high side. My doctor wants me to aim for below 130/80 mmHg to keep my risk of heart issues lower. I've been keeping track of it at home, and my readings fluctuate between 135-140 systolic and 80-90 diastolic, depending on my stress levels and salt intake. I'm trying to cut back on sodium and drink more water, which seems to help.One test that surprised me was my vitamin D levels. I thought I was getting enough sunlight, but my levels came back at 22 ng/mL, which is considered deficient. The normal range is 30-50 ng/mL, so my doctor put me on a vitamin D supplement. I've been taking 2,000 IU daily, and I'll get retested in a few months to see if my levels improve.Oh! And my thyroid numbers were stable this time, which was a relief. My TSH was 2.1 mIU/L, which is right in the normal range(0.5-4.5 mIU/L). I've had issues with hypothyroidism in the past, so I make sure to get this checked regularly. My T4 levels were also good at 1.2 ng/dL, meaning my current dosage of levothyroxine is working well.My bone density scan showed a slight decline. My T-score for my spine was -1.8, which is considered osteopenia(the stage before osteoporosis). My hip T-score was -1.5, which is also in the borderline range. My doctor advised me to keep up with strength training and calcium intake to prevent further bone loss. I've started adding more dairy and leafy greens to my diet, plus I take a calcium supplement with vitamin K2 to help with absorption.Liver and kidney function tests were mostly fine, but my ALT levels were a little elevated at 42 U/L(normal is under 35 U/L). My doctor thinks it might be related to some recent medication adjustments, so we're going to keep an eye on it. My creatinine levels were at 0.9 mg/dL, which is well within the normal range(0.6-1.2 mg/dL), so no concerns with kidney function.One thing I was really curious about was my inflammatory markers. My C-reactive protein(CRP) was at 3.2 mg/L, which is slightly elevated(ideal is under 3.0 mg/L), indicating some mild inflammation—probably related to my osteoarthritis. My ESR(erythrocyte sedimentation rate) was 18 mm/hr, which is within the normal range(0-20 mm/hr), so at least there's no major inflammation going on.Overall, I'm feeling good about my latest test results, but there are definitely things I need to work on—mainly keeping my blood sugar in check and getting my vitamin D levels up. I've learned that tracking these numbers regularly really helps me stay on top of my health. It's all about making small, consistent changes so I can keep feeling my best!I have been taking levothyroxine for my hypothyroidism for several years. My doctor has adjusted my dosage a few times to get it just right. I also take a calcium supplement with vitamin K2 to help with bone health, as I have osteoporosis. For my osteoarthritis, I take a combination of pain relievers and anti-inflammatory medications. My diabetes is managed with metformin and insulin. I also take medication for my hypertension, which includes a combination of diuretics and beta blockers. It's a lot to keep track of, but I make sure to take my medications as prescribed and attend regular check-ups with my doctor to monitor my progress.
